code: zoo_report <- report_interactions(zoo_est, classes = classify_interactions(zoo_est),                                   agreement = compare_null_models(zoo_est)) cat(zoo_report$methods, sep = "\n\n") #> The experiment combined 2 stressors, imidacloprid (absent and applied, with absent as control) and temperature (ambient, elevated and heatwaves, with ambient as control), in a full factorial design (6 treatment combinations), with 4 experimental units (mesocosm) per combination, sampled at 7 times (day -1, 10, 24, 38, 52, 66 and 80). The sampling before the stressors were applied (day -1) was not tested. The design identified 2 contrast sets: 2 pairwise interactions. #>  #> The analysis was run with the R package must 0.3.0 (Amador Crespo & Rico 2026) in R 4.6.2 (R Core Team 2026). The response (total_density) was modelled with a generalized linear mixed model with one mean per treatment combination and sampling time (a cell-means model) and a random intercept for each mesocosm, fitted by maximum likelihood with glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 (Brooks et al. 2017). The error distribution was chosen among candidates suited to the values of the response (Gaussian (identity link), Gaussian (log link), Gamma (log link) and lognormal (log link)): the candidate that converged with a positive-definite Hessian and had the lowest AIC was selected. The model selected was Gamma (log link). For the inference, the selected model was refitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML). #>  #> Each interaction was tested against simple addition (AD), the multiplicative model (MU) and dominance (DO). The null models were chosen with the guidelines of Schäfer & Piggott (2018), in which must adds two conditions: concentration addition requires that the stressors alone act in the same direction, and stress addition that none of them increases the response. The authors stated that the stressors do not act similarly, one of them acts specifically on physiology, the effect is not mortality and the stressor-effect relationships are not known. They did not state whether the distribution of sensitivities is known or how the sensitivities are correlated. The criteria that depend on the effects of the stressors alone (whether one effect reaches 90% of the effect limit, whether their sum exceeds the limit, whether a stressor alone increases the response and whether two act in opposite directions) were evaluated from the effects estimated by the models in each contrast set and sampling time, with 95% intervals; a criterion was not known when the interval spanned its threshold. Each criterion that was not known (or that differed among contrast sets) took each of its values, and every null model reached was kept. #>  #> Following Madge Pimentel et al. (2025), each interaction was computed from the means predicted by the model with the random effects at zero (post-estimation inference), as the deviation of the combination of stressors from the expectation of the null model, as a difference on the scale of the response (AD and DO) and as a difference on the log scale (MU). Uncertainty was obtained from 4,000 draws of the fixed effects from their estimated distribution (Krinsky & Robb 1986), which gave percentile intervals and two-sided p-values. To correct for small samples, the covariance came from the REML refit and the distributions were t, with the degrees of freedom given by the replication of the experimental units (18). Intervals were computed at the 95% level, and p-values were adjusted for the false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995) within each response, null model and estimate, across contrast sets and sampling times; effects averaged over the sampling times were tested and adjusted separately. Each interaction was also tested for equivalence with two one-sided tests (Schuirmann 1987) of whether its deviation relative to the response of the reference combination, (observed - expected) / reference, lay between -0.5 and 0.5; each test measured the signed distance of the means from the closest means at the bound, on a scale that stabilizes their variance (Anscombe 1948). Random numbers were generated with seed 2024. #>  #> Interactions were classified with the directional scheme of Piggott et al. (2015): each single, combined and interaction effect was coded as positive, negative or not significant from its adjusted p-value (alpha = 0.05), and each net interaction was classed as additive (no deviation detected), as a positive or negative synergism or as a positive or negative antagonism (their Table 1). Dominance, which does not predict the combination from the single effects, was not classified. With the equivalence margin, each net interaction was also a deviation, a negligible deviation (detected but within the margin), equivalent (no deviation detected and within the margin) or inconclusive. Across the null models compared (AD, MU and DO), an interaction was robust when every null model tested flagged a deviation with the same sign (adjusted p < 0.05), dependent on the null model when only some did, and conflicting when they flagged deviations of opposite sign. zoo_report$decisions[!zoo_report$decisions$source %in% c("default", "recorded"),                      c("decision", code: report <- report_interactions(est, classes = cls) cat(report$methods, sep = "\n\n") #> The experiment combined 3 stressors, insecticide (absent and chlorpyrifos, with absent as control), herbicide (absent and diuron, with absent as control) and nutrients (ambient and added, with ambient as control), in a full factorial design (8 treatment combinations), with 3 experimental units (mesocosm) per combination, sampled at 4 times (day 7, 14, 30 and 50). The design identified 4 contrast sets: 3 pairwise interactions and 1 three-way interaction, with the stressors outside each set at their control. #>  #> The analysis was run with the R package must 0.3.0 (Amador Crespo & Rico 2026) in R 4.6.2 (R Core Team 2026). Each response (total_density, cyclopoida and daphnia) was modelled with a generalized linear mixed model with one mean per treatment combination and sampling time (a cell-means model) and a random intercept for each mesocosm, fitted by maximum likelihood with glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 (Brooks et al. 2017). The error distribution was chosen among candidates suited to the values of each response (Gaussian (identity link), Gaussian (log link), Gamma (log link) and lognormal (log link), for total_density; Gaussian (identity link), Gaussian (log link) and Tweedie (log link), for cyclopoida and daphnia): the candidate that converged with a positive-definite Hessian and had the lowest AIC was selected. The models selected were Gamma (log link) for total_density; Tweedie (log link) for cyclopoida and daphnia. The means of the treatment combinations with only zeros (6 for daphnia) were fixed at the boundary of the link function; a contrast that compares such a combination with its expectation was tested from the probability of observing only zeros under that expectation, and contrasts that need such a combination to compute it were not estimated. For the inference, the selected models were refitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML). #>  #> Each interaction was tested against simple addition (AD), the multiplicative model (MU) and dominance (DO). The null models were chosen with the guidelines of Schäfer & Piggott (2018), in which must adds two conditions: concentration addition requires that the stressors alone act in the same direction, and stress addition that none of them increases the response. The authors stated that the stressors do not act similarly, one of them acts specifically on physiology, the effect is not mortality and the stressor-effect relationships are not known. They did not state whether the distribution of sensitivities is known or how the sensitivities are correlated. The criteria that depend on the effects of the stressors alone (whether one effect reaches 90% of the effect limit, whether their sum exceeds the limit, whether a stressor alone increases the response and whether two act in opposite directions) were evaluated from the effects estimated by the models in each contrast set and sampling time, with 95% intervals; a criterion was not known when the interval spanned its threshold. Each criterion that was not known (or that differed among contrast sets) took each of its values, and every null model reached was kept. #>  #> Following Madge Pimentel et al. (2025), each interaction was computed from the means predicted by the models with the random effects at zero (post-estimation inference), as the deviation of the combination of stressors from the expectation of the null model, as a difference on the scale of the response (AD and DO) and as a difference on the log scale (MU). For sets of three or more stressors, both the net deviation from the single effects and the pure highest-order interaction (under AD and MU) were estimated. Dominance is defined for two stressors only. Uncertainty was obtained from 4,000 draws of the fixed effects from their estimated distribution (Krinsky & Robb 1986), which gave percentile intervals and two-sided p-values. To correct for small samples, the covariance came from the REML refit and the distributions were t, with the degrees of freedom given by the replication of the experimental units (16). Intervals were computed at the 95% level, and p-values were adjusted for the false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995) within each response, null model and estimate, across contrast sets and sampling times; effects averaged over the sampling times were tested and adjusted separately. Random numbers were generated with seed 2021. #>  #> Interactions were classified with the directional scheme of Piggott et al. (2015): each single, combined and interaction effect was coded as positive, negative or not significant from its adjusted p-value (alpha = 0.05), and each net interaction was classed as additive (no deviation detected), as a positive or negative synergism or as a positive or negative antagonism (their Table 1). Dominance, which does not predict the combination from the single effects, was not classified. For three or more stressors, the same rules were applied to the net deviation and the single effects of all the stressors of the set; pure interactions were not classified. changed <- code: jars <- expand.grid(   salinity = c("ambient", "high"),   warming = c("no", "yes"),   replicate = 1:5,   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) jars$jar <- seq_len(nrow(jars)) mu <- 40 * ifelse(jars$salinity == "high", 0.5, 1) *   ifelse(jars$warming == "yes", 0.5, 1) jars$algae <- stats::qpois(c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8)[jars$replicate], mu) design <- describe_design(jars, c("salinity", "warming"),   control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "jar") fits <- fit_responses(jars, "algae", design, residual_checks = FALSE,   seed = 1, quiet = TRUE) # Simple addition (the default) est <- estimate_interactions(fits, n_sim = 2000, seed = 1) est #> <must_interactions> 1 response(s); null models: AD #> Inference: Krinsky-Robb simulation (2000 draws), small-sample correction (REML, t); 95% intervals; p-values adjusted with BH; seed 1 #> Scales: AD = differences (response scale) #> Interactions (1 rows): #>  response                 combination model estimand estimate lower upper df #>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    AD      net      9.8 0.783  19.3 16 #>  p_adj status #>  0.035     ok est$estimates[est$estimates$component == "interaction",   c("null_model", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "df", "p_adjusted")] #>   null_model estimate    lower    upper df p_adjusted #> 4         AD      9.8 0.782748 19.30277 16      0.035 # The three null models and the procedure of Madge Pimentel et al. (2025), # without the correction estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = c("AD", "MU", "DO"), n_sim = 2000,   seed = 1, correction = "none") #> <must_interactions> 1 response(s); null models: AD, MU, DO #> Inference: Krinsky-Robb simulation (2000 draws), no small-sample correction; 95% intervals; p-values adjusted with BH; seed 1 #> Scales: AD = differences (response scale); MU = log ratios; DO = dominance (response scale) #> Interactions (3 rows): #>  response                 combination model estimand  estimate   lower  upper #>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    AD      net   9.80000   1.470 18.500 #>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    MU      net  -0.00501  -0.413  0.413 #>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    DO      net -10.00000 -12.800 -4.730 #>   df  p_adj status #>  Inf 0.0160     ok #>  Inf 0.9700     ok #>  Inf 0.0005     ok # Additive, or only not detected? An equivalence margin of 10% of the control eq <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = c("AD", "MU"), n_sim = 2000, seed = 1,   margin = 0.1) eq$estimates[eq$estimates$component == "interaction",   c("null_model", "relative", "relative_lower", "relative_upper", "p_equivalence")] #>   null_model     relative relative_lower relative_upper p_equivalence #> 4         AD  0.246231156     0.02237831      0.4369641     0.9145769 #> 8         MU -0.001262594    -0.12707548      0.1096770     0.0560537 classify_interactions(eq)[, c("null_model", "class", "verdict")] #>   null_model class      verdict #> 1         AD    -A    deviation #> 2         MU    AD inconclusive # Bliss independence, with its rescaled interaction bl <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = "BL", n_sim = 2000, seed = 1) bl$estimates[bl$estimates$component == "interaction",   c("estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_value", "rescaled", "rescaled_class")] #>       estimate      lower    upper p_value rescaled rescaled_class #> 4 -0.001262594 -0.1270755 0.109677   0.966   -0.005       additive # A model fitted outside must model <- stats::glm(algae ~ salinity * warming, family = stats::poisson(), data = jars) estimate_interactions(model, design, null_models = c("AD", "MU", "BL"), n_sim = 2000,   seed = 1) #> <must_interactions> 1 response(s); null models: AD, MU, BL #> Model: glm, poisson (log); means from emmeans #> Inference: Krinsky-Robb simulation (2000 draws), degrees of freedom from emmeans; 95% intervals; p-values adjusted with BH; code: jars <- expand.grid(   salinity = c("ambient", "high"),   warming = c("no", "yes"),   replicate = 1:5,   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) jars$jar <- seq_len(nrow(jars)) mu <- 40 * ifelse(jars$salinity == "high", 0.5, 1) *   ifelse(jars$warming == "yes", 0.5, 1) jars$algae <- stats::qpois(c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8)[jars$replicate], mu) design <- describe_design(jars, c("salinity", "warming"),   control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "jar") fits <- fit_responses(jars, "algae", design, residual_checks = FALSE,   seed = 1, quiet = TRUE) est <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = c("AD", "MU"), n_sim = 2000, seed = 1) summary(est) #> Interactions: Krinsky-Robb simulation; small-sample correction; adjusted p-values (BH) below 0.05 #> Deviating / tested interactions by sampling time: #>  response model estimand all #>     algae    AD      net 1/1 #>     algae    MU      net 0/1 #>  #> Classes of the net deviations (Piggott et al. 2015) by sampling time: #>  response model  all #>     algae    AD 1 -A #>     algae    MU 1 AD #>  #> Agreement between null models (AD, MU), robust/model-dependent/conflicting/none: #>  response estimand     all #>     algae      net 0/1/0/0 #>  #> Counts of boundary tests and of rows not estimated: `$interactions`; classes: `$classes`.

code: jars <- expand.grid(   salinity = c("ambient", "high"),   warming = c("no", "yes"),   replicate = 1:5,   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) jars$jar <- seq_len(nrow(jars)) mu <- 40 * ifelse(jars$salinity == "high", 0.5, 1) *   ifelse(jars$warming == "yes", 0.5, 1) jars$algae <- stats::qpois(c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8)[jars$replicate], mu) design <- describe_design(jars, c("salinity", "warming"),   control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "jar") fits <- fit_responses(jars, "algae", design, residual_checks = FALSE,   seed = 1, quiet = TRUE) est <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = c("AD", "MU"), n_sim = 2000,   seed = 1) report <- report_interactions(est, classes = classify_interactions(est)) report #> <must_report> #> Methods #>  #> The experiment combined 2 stressors, salinity (ambient and high, with ambient #> as control) and warming (no and yes, with no as control), in a full factorial #> design (4 treatment combinations), with 5 experimental units (jar) per #> combination. The design identified one contrast set, a pairwise interaction. #>  #> The analysis was run with the R package must 0.3.0 (Amador Crespo & Rico 2026) #> in R 4.6.2 (R Core Team 2026). The response (algae) was modelled with a #> generalized linear model with one mean per treatment combination (a cell-means #> model), fitted by maximum likelihood with glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 (Brooks et al. #> 2017). The error distribution was chosen among candidates suited to the values #> of the response (Poisson (log link) and negative binomial (NB2, log link)): the #> candidate that converged with a positive-definite Hessian and had the lowest #> AIC was selected, except that the Poisson was used only if the negative #> binomial did not converge. The model selected was negative binomial (NB2, log #> link). For the inference, the selected model was refitted by restricted maximum #> likelihood (REML). #>  #> Each interaction was tested against simple addition (AD) and the multiplicative #> model (MU). Following Madge Pimentel et al. (2025), each interaction was #> computed from the means predicted by the model (post-estimation inference), as #> the deviation of the combination of stressors from the expectation of the null #> model, as a difference on the scale of the response (AD) and as a difference on #> the log scale (MU). Uncertainty was obtained from 2,000 draws of the fixed #> effects from their estimated distribution (Krinsky & Robb 1986), which gave #> percentile intervals and two-sided p-values. To correct for small samples, the #> covariance came from the REML refit and the distributions were t, with the #> degrees of freedom given by the replication of the experimental units (16). #> Intervals were computed at the 95% level, and p-values were adjusted for the #> false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995) within each response, null #> model and estimate, across contrast sets. Random numbers were generated with #> seed 1. #>  #> Interactions were classified with the directional scheme of Piggott et al. #> (2015): each single, combined and interaction effect was coded as positive, #> negative or not significant from its adjusted p-value (alpha = 0.05), and each #> net interaction was classed as additive (no deviation detected), as a positive #> or negative synergism or as a positive or negative antagonism (their Table 1). #>  #> Decisions #>  #> describe_design() #>   Stressors and their control levels: salinity (control ambient), warming #>     (control no) Markdown, for an R Markdown document (in a chunk with results = "asis") cat(format(report, format = "markdown"), sep = "\n") #> The experiment combined 2 stressors, salinity (ambient and high, with ambient as control) and warming (no and yes, with no as control), in a full factorial design (4 treatment combinations), with 5 experimental units (jar) per combination. The design identified one contrast set, a pairwise interaction. #>  #> The analysis was run with the R package must 0.3.0 (Amador Crespo & Rico 2026) in R 4.6.2 (R Core Team 2026). The response (algae) was modelled with a generalized linear model with one mean per treatment combination (a cell-means model), fitted by maximum likelihood with glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 (Brooks et al. 2017). The error distribution was chosen among candidates suited to the values of the response (Poisson (log link) and negative binomial (NB2, log link)): the candidate that converged with a positive-definite Hessian and had the lowest AIC was selected, except that the Poisson was used only if the negative binomial did not converge. The model selected was negative binomial (NB2, log link). For the inference, the selected model was refitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML). #>  #> Each interaction was tested against simple addition (AD) and the multiplicative model (MU). Following Madge Pimentel et al. (2025), each interaction was computed from the means predicted by the model (post-estimation inference), as the deviation of the combination of stressors from the expectation of the null model, as a difference on the scale of the response (AD) and as a difference on the log scale (MU). Uncertainty was obtained from 2,000 draws of the fixed effects from their estimated distribution (Krinsky & Robb 1986), which gave percentile intervals and two-sided p-values. To correct for small samples, the covariance came from the REML refit and the distributions were t, with the degrees of freedom given by the replication of the experimental units (16). Intervals were computed at the 95% level, and p-values were adjusted for the false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995) within each response, null model and estimate, across contrast sets. Random numbers were generated with seed 1. #>  #> Interactions were classified with the directional scheme of Piggott et al. (2015): each single, combined and interaction effect was coded as positive, negative or not significant from its adjusted p-value (alpha = 0.05), and each net interaction was classed as additive (no deviation detected), as a positive or negative synergism or as a positive or negative antagonism (their Table 1). #>  #> | Step | Decision | Argument | Value | Default | Source | #> Step 4: the sensitivities are highly #>     negatively correlated and the sum of the effects is below the #>     effect limit; step 7: none of the earlier steps applies. #>   MU (multiplicative): excluded. The multiplicative model needs #>     mortality as the effect (step 5) or the sum of the effects above #>     the effect limit (step 6), but the effect is not mortality and the #>     sum of the effects does not exceed the effect limit. #>   DO (dominance): possible. Step 3: the sensitivities are highly #>     positively correlated, or the effect of one stressor is close to #>     the effect limit. #>   SAM (stress addition): excluded. The stress addition model needs one #>     stressor that acts specifically on physiology, mortality as the #>     effect, stressors that do not increase the response and a known #>     stressor-effect relationship or sensitivity distribution (step 2), #>     but the effect is not mortality. #>   CA (concentration addition): excluded. Concentration addition needs #>     stressors that act similarly, with effects in the same direction, #>     and a known stressor-effect relationship (step 1), but the #>     stressors do not act similarly and their stressor-effect #>     relationship is not known. #> Unknown criteria that would change the choice: #>   Correlation of the sensitivities (`correlation`): positive -> DO; #>     negative -> AD; weak -> AD #> For estimate_interactions(): null_models = c("AD", "DO") # The same, with an effect close to the effect limit suggest_null_models(similar_action = FALSE, mortality = FALSE,   stressor_effect = FALSE, effects = c(salinity = 0.3, warming = 0.95)) #> <must_null_models> after the guidelines of Schäfer and Piggott (2018), Fig. 3 #> Criteria: #>   The stressors act similarly (same mode of action)                       no #>   One stressor acts specifically on physiology                            unknown #>   The effect is mortality                                                 no #>   The stressor-effect relationship is known                               no #>   The sensitivity distribution is known                                   unknown #>   Correlation of the sensitivities                                        unknown #>   The effect of one stressor is close to the effect limit (at least 90%)  yes #>   The sum of the effects compared with the effect limit                   above #>   A stressor alone increases the response                                 no #>   Stressors alone with opposite effects                                   no #> Effects of the stressors alone (given): salinity = 0.30 (decrease), #>   warming = 0.95 (decrease); type: double negative. #> Null models: #>   AD (simple addition): excluded.
